headline: Microsoft Paint used to run the original Doom engine at up to 35 FPS
summary: A Microsoft Azure CTO has released a project that uses MS Paint as a monitor for the classic first-person shooter, achieving playable frame rates.
details: A new project called DoomPaint allows the original Doom engine to run using Microsoft Paint as its display. Developed by Mark Russinovich, Microsoft's CTO for Azure, this unique 'port' utilizes an OLE clipboard hack to render each frame within Paint.

The project successfully runs the shareware version of DOOM1.WAD, with Freedoom WADs filling in for missing episodes. The game renders headlessly, with frames captured and pasted into Paint as document edits. Russinovich notes that the "relatively low frame rate is part of the charm," but it can reach up to 35 FPS.

While the frame rate can fluctuate, potentially dropping to "spreadsheet-tier" performance, achieving 35 FPS at resolutions like 320x200 or even 640x400 is remarkable for this method. The project even includes sound and music support.

Russinovich clarifies that Paint acts solely as the visual output, stating, "Paint renders the game but does not compute it. Paint computes nothing." The DoomPaint project is available under the MIT license, with instructions and resources provided on its GitHub page.

This creative endeavor comes from Russinovich, a key figure at Microsoft known for his work on SysInternals and shaping Azure's architecture. His involvement in such a playful, retro-computing project highlights the enduring appeal of classic games and ingenious coding solutions.

headline_marked: [[RTX 5060 Ti]] survives car crash after being bent in half
headline: RTX 5060 Ti survives car crash after being bent in half
summary: A GPU bent in half after a car crash was repaired with a simple memory chip resolder, restoring full performance and stability.
details: An AX Gaming RTX 5060 Ti, purchased by a customer in China, was involved in a severe car crash that totaled the vehicle. Miraculously, the graphics card survived the incident with minimal damage.
Despite being bent in half, the card's short PCB design meant the internal components were largely unaffected. The technician, Brother Zhang, found no short circuits on the power rails.
Initial testing of the bare PCB showed the GPU was functional. However, driver installation caused system instability and black screens, indicating a subtle issue.
Upon closer inspection, Brother Zhang identified and resoldered a memory module near the PCB's flex point. This crucial repair restored the card's full 8GB of VRAM and stability.
After the resolder, the RTX 5060 Ti passed benchmarks with a 98.9% stability score in 3DMark and peaked at 67°C in Furmark, proving its resilience and repairability.
caption:
A graphics card bent in half after a car crash was brought back to life with a simple resolder.

An AX Gaming RTX 5060 Ti, purchased by a customer in China, was involved in a severe car crash that totaled the vehicle. Miraculously, the graphics card survived the incident with minimal damage.

Despite being bent in half, the card's short PCB design meant the internal components were largely unaffected. The technician, Brother Zhang, found no short circuits on the power rails.

Initial testing of the bare PCB showed the GPU was functional. However, driver installation caused system instability and black screens, indicating a subtle issue.

Upon closer inspection, Brother Zhang identified and resoldered a memory module near the PCB's flex point. This crucial repair restored the card's full 8GB of VRAM and stability.

After the resolder, the RTX 5060 Ti passed benchmarks with a 98.9% stability score in 3DMark and peaked at 67°C in Furmark, proving its resilience and repairability.
